# Engine Flushes and High-Mileage Engines: A Cautionary Tale from a VQ35DE Swap

Catastrophic engine failure following routine maintenance is a nightmare scenario, but the technical mechanics behind it can be surprisingly predictable for those who understand fluid dynamics and oil system architecture. The case of a 2006 Infiniti G35 Coupe with a VQ35DE engine illustrates exactly why "engine flushes" are often advised against on high-mileage vehicles, even when performed by reputable shops like Kwik Kar.

The specific failure mode describedâa thrown rod leading to an oil blowoutâis a classic symptom of debris-induced wear. The vehicle in question had accumulated approximately 100,000 miles prior to the service. While both owners were diligent about using synthetic Mobil 1 and performing timely changes, the internal condition of the engine was likely not pristine. High-mileage engines often accumulate sludge and varnish in critical oil passages, such as the main and rod bearings.

The immediate trigger for failure was the introduction of an aggressive solvent-based flush additive. Unlike a mild detergent found in standard oil changes, these products are designed to loosen decades of accumulated deposits. When the engine is run immediately after adding this solvent, those loosened particles do not simply disappear; they settle into the oil pan. As the oil pump circulates this mixture, it acts like a high-pressure slurry grinder. This abrasive mix can scour bearing surfaces or, more dangerously, clog restrictive oil galleries that have been relying on the existing sludge to keep moving parts lubricated until a proper filter change occurs.

The symptoms reportedâinitially an obnoxious rattle at startup followed by low oil levels and dark fluidâare consistent with debris migration. The mechanic's attempt to mitigate the noise with an STP additive was ineffective because once metal-on-metal contact has occurred or bearings are compromised, chemical additives cannot repair physical damage. The fact that the car ran for another 2,000 miles before the catastrophic failure suggests the engine was running on a compromised foundation, eventually leading to the rod throw.

When evaluating repair options, cost-benefit analysis becomes critical. Replacing the engine at Kwik Kar for approximately $9,800 using a used unit with over 90,000 miles introduces significant risk. A high-mileage donor engine may have existing wear patterns that will lead to premature failure again, negating the cost savings of avoiding new parts. Conversely, sourcing a remanufactured engine online for $2,000â$3,000 offers a much higher likelihood of long-term reliability. However, this path requires technical competence and specific shop partnerships.

Most independent shops will not install a customer-provided engine due to liability concerns regarding the core unit's history. Finding a facility in the north DFW area willing to perform labor-only installation for a third-party engine is a non-trivial task. If you proceed with a swap, ensure the new block and head are compatible with your specific transmission bell housing pattern and that all ancillary mounts (timing chain guides, tensioner rails) match your original specifications.

The lesson here extends beyond one specific incident: on high-mileage engines, the philosophy of "cleaning" the system often does more harm than good. If an engine has been running well without issues, the risk profile of introducing aggressive solvents outweighs the theoretical benefit of removing sludge. Always prioritize mechanical integrity over chemical cleaning agents when dealing with older powertrains.
